_comment: The second skill, and the format's first real test. beat-montage's
manifest says every field earned its place by being something the
by-hand build could not do without, and that the fields a SECOND skill
turns out to need should be added then rather than designed now.
This one needed one field added and one field omitted. Both are
explained where they appear, because the interesting thing about a
format's second user is what it got wrong the first time.
name: Tutorial
summary: Turns a screen recording into a finished tutorial: hard cuts between framings, an inset frame on a light backdrop, the camera full frame over a spoken introduction and over pauses, captions.
_noTemplate: beat-montage ships template.kerf and opens it as its first recipe step,
so that a fumbled run still leaves a real project on the timeline. This
skill deliberately ships NONE, and shipping one would be worse than
· The canvas is not knowable in advance. It is cut to the recorded
display's own aspect ratio so the picture is neither cropped nor
letterboxed, and that number comes out of the take.
first act, because a take must not stack on top of whatever was
open. Any template would be wiped one call later.
So the safety net is somewhere else, and it is real: the tool has a
`raw` mode that lays the take down with no interpretation at all, and
the recorder offers `Open raw` beside `Open with the Tutorial skill`.
The buyer's floor is their own footage on a timeline, which is a
better floor than somebody else's title card.
_trial: The second field this skill added, and the reason the trial system
exists at all: a publisher says how many times their skill may be run
before it is bought, and `electron/skillTrials.ts` counts.
Zero here, and zero means NOT GATED. This skill ships inside Kerf, so
counting runs of it would be gating somebody out of something they
already have. The field is declared anyway rather than omitted,
because 'no trial' and 'nobody thought about it' should not look the
What the count is worth, stated where a publisher will read it: the
ledger is sealed with AES-GCM and held 0600, so it is tamper-EVIDENT —
an edited file fails to decrypt and is then treated as SPENT rather
than as fresh, which is the decision the whole thing turns on. It is
not tamper-PROOF: deleting the ledger resets the count on that
machine, and nothing that also lives on that machine can prevent it.
The durable version is server-side against an account, which the
store already has the tables for and which is not built yet.
_assets: None, and this is the field that changed. beat-montage ships a music
bed because a montage needs music it did not record. Everything this
skill needs, it either finds in the take or SYNTHESISES: the click
ticks and the zoom air are rendered from oscillators and noise by
sfxEngine at build time and written into the take's own folder, so
they travel with the recording rather than with the skill. Nothing to
license, nothing to download, nothing to 404.

slots.description: A take folder written by Kerf's screen recorder, holding screen.mp4 and cursor.json. An optional transcript.json beside them is used instead of transcribing, which is what a scripted tutorial already has.
Transcribe the narration on device. The words also decide where the camera cuts, so turning this off changes more than the captions.
How far the frame CUTS in on a click. 2.8 is the reference video's own figure, measured; 1.5 is a nudge, 3 is the ceiling.

The spoken language, or `auto` to detect it. This decides more than the captions: the words are what place the camera cuts and what says whether the take opens with an introduction, so decoding the wrong language loses the edit rather than just the subtitles.

Spell-check the transcript with the agent CLI already configured in Kerf before the words go on screen: misspellings, word boundaries, punctuation, in the SAME language. It is only ever allowed to correct a line, never to rewrite one, and a reply that grows a line into a sentence nobody said is refused whole. This does NOT control the audit: repetition loops, non-speech markers and stutters are found and removed with no model at all, because those are deletions and a model asked to fill that hole will invent fluent narration instead.

What the inset picture sits on. The first five are light — the look every screen-tutorial tool ships — and `daylight` is the reference video's own backdrop, measured off it. The last three are dark, for a dark-theme subject.

_slots: `kind: enum` with an `options` list is the one field this skill added.
beat-montage's slots are a folder and a string, and neither needed a
vocabulary; a backdrop with four values and no list would be a free
text field that fails on the fifth character somebody types.
`targetClipName` is absent throughout, and that is the other thing a
second skill teaches: it exists to find a slot's clip inside a
TEMPLATE. With no template there is nothing to point at, so the slots
here are all arguments rather than substitutions.
`requiresSlot` is the field the THIRD pass added, and it was added
because the same gap turned up three times rather than because it
looked tidy. `language` is meaningless with `captions: false`, and so
is `cleanCaptions`, and so is the camera opening on an introduction,
which is decided from the words and is not even a slot. Before this
field a caller could set the spoken language, get no captions, and
have nothing anywhere tell them the two settings were related.
It says DEPENDENCY, not validation: a dependent slot with its parent
off is inert rather than an error, because refusing the combination
would break every caller that sets a language once and toggles
captions per take. What it buys is that an interface can grey the
slot out and an agent can be told why the argument it passed did
nothing.
_recipe: One step, and that is the point rather than a shortcut. The work is
not a sequence of independent edits that happen to run in order: the
transcript has to exist before the camera cuts are placed, because it
is the only signal that knows where a sentence ends, and the cuts have
to exist before the zooms can chain around them. A recipe that
exposed those as three steps would let a caller run them in an order
that cannot work, and call the result a skill.
_verify: 13 checks, every one against an artifact rather than a return value.
The take it runs on is SYNTHESISED with ffmpeg to have known colours —
a dark red screen with one bright green square in a corner, and a
solid blue camera — so that every claim the skill makes can be
measured as a change in what is on the canvas:
· the zoom is real, because the green square occupies several times
more of the frame at the moment of the click than it does at rest;
· it is aimed, because the square lands near the CENTRE rather than
· the camera takeover is real, because the frame is blue during the
pause and is not blue on either side of it;
· the frame is inset, because the backdrop is visible at the edges
at rest and gone once the zoom is in;
· and the sounds are real files on the timeline, not a count.
The colours are the method, not a convenience. A montage that reported
fifteen shots on the beat while rendering fifteen seconds of black has
happened in this codebase, and every suite here has been written since
on the rule that a tool's own report is not evidence.
_notInHereYet: Still absent, and still deliberately: no dependency graph (one step),
no pricing or entitlement (that is the store), and no install
lifecycle. New this time and worth naming: no way to declare a
REQUIREMENT that is not a tool. This skill is better with Whisper
installed and works without it, and the manifest has nowhere to say
so — `requiresTools` is a hard list, and 'better with' is not that.
The tool reports it at runtime instead. If a third skill needs the
same thing, that is when the field should exist.
